source: RFC 0014 R7 (mixed-version compatibility; the coordinator's decisions of 2026-11-24 on R, W and the web server's limit); the compatibility review of 2026-11-24 (F3, CE-4)
statement: The CoSec-Identity header has two limits. R, the largest header a reader accepts by default (`cosec.pipeline.identity.max-size`, IdentityCodec.READ_MAX_BYTES, 8 KB), is never lowered within 8.x. W, the largest header CoSec's writers write by default (`cosec.gateway.identity.max-size` and HttpControlService's relay of a request's caller, IdentityCodec.WRITE_MAX_BYTES, 6 KB), is below R by the room the members a later 8.x version adds may take: a later version may raise W, up to R and never past it, so an 8.x reader at its default reads what any 8.x writer writes at its default; a header over a writer's limit fails the request (500) or the call before it is sent, never cut short. Spring Boot's servers count every request header against `server.max-http-request-header-size` (8 KB by default on Tomcat and Reactor Netty), so on a host that reads the identity (cosec.pipeline.mode=gateway, or cosec.pipeline.caller=forwarded-identity) the starter derives that limit when the operator has not set it: R and 8 KB for the request's other headers, 16 KB at the defaults, named at startup with what it is derived from; the control API's service port, the application's server on another port (CTL-71), has the same limit. An operator's value is kept; one below R and 8 KB is named at startup at WARN with both numbers, and the host still starts. A process that holds both limits holds W to R: a host that reads the identity and relays its callers with HttpControlService does not start when its R is below the relay's W (it would relay headers larger than its own gate admits), and a gateway whose `cosec.gateway.identity.max-size` is above the R every 8.x service reads by default is named at startup at WARN with both numbers.
